newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian coal miners' leaders order end to strike.
newsitem.headline: Russian coal miners' leaders order end to strike.

text.p: Russian trade union leaders ordered a halt to a nationwide coal miners' strike from Thursday after the government promised to pay huge wage arrears, but some miners refused to return to work.

The leadership of the Rosugleprof miners' trade union announced late on Wednesday they were suspending the strike, which began on December 3, after Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin vowed to settle wage debts by December 27.

The miners, some of whom have not been paid since June, have exacerbated problems for Chernomyrdin, opening him to fierce attacks in parliament over his handling of the crisis and deepening already widespread public discontent.

His problems may not be over. In a sign of defiance, strike committees in the Rostov, Gukov and Tula regions of western and southern Russia decided to stay on strike until they received their wages, RIA news agency said.
Itar-Tass news agency said miners in Rostov would decide later on Thursday whether to go back to work but RIA said the strike committees, representing 70,000 workers at 43 pits, were standing firm.

"Unless their problems are solved, the miners of the Rostov region threaten to begin a civil disobedience action on December 15 and block traffic on the North Caucasian railway," RIA said, referring to railways in one of Russia's most troubled areas.
Six miners told Ekho Moskvy radio station they were going on a hunger strike until the government settled its wage debts.

"When wage arrears go back for four or five months, the situation is not normal. They (the authorities) laugh at the workers, make fun of them," said Alexander Dyakov, arom the town of Leninsk-Kuznetsk in the major Kuzbass mining region.

At its high point, union leaders said up to 400,000 miners in nearly 200 pits and open-cast mines were on strike. The strike has wavered since then, with some miners going back to work, partly to maintain the safety of their pits.
The union says the government debt to the industry is more than two trillion roubles ($400 million) and that even bigger company debts have led to huge delays in paying out wages.
Nikolai Antonov, an official at the Rosugol coal company, told Interfax news agency that he doubted whether all miners could receive all their back pay by the end of December.
The commercial television channel NTV reported from Kuzbass that it was not clear how miners there had reacted to the call to suspend the strike because Thursday was a national holiday.
But NTV correspondent Alexander Kolpakov pointed out in a report from Kemerovo, the region's main town, that the miners had paid little heed to orders from Moscow in the past.

The communist-led opposition has used the strike to attack the government in debates in the State Duma, the lower house of parliament, on the draft 1997 budget. The chamber is expected to vote on whether to approve the budget on Sunday.
The upper house, usually loyal to Chernomyrdin and President Boris Yeltsin, has also turned against the prime minister.
It has demanded an urgent improvement in the government's work, despite his pleas that wage delays are partly caused by widespread tax evasion leaving state coffers bare.
Pro-democracy strikes by coal miners in 1989 and 1990 helped Yeltsin in his struggle against the communist administration which ended with the collapse of the Soviet Union in late 1991.

But tough economic reforms since then have been damaging for the mines, most of which are loss-making. Since reconstruction started in the coal sector in 1993, the government has closed 50 unprofitable mines and plans to shut more than 60 others soon.
